arguments.premise_synthesis: Gold has historically been a good store of value and could be transferred digitally. Bitcoin offers a public, transparent, decentralized ledger with pseudonymity. People are currently hoarding gold and Bitcoin as stores of value. Central bank gold holdings have surpassed US treasuries for the first time in 50 years, indicating a shift away from the dollar. Gresham's law (bad money drives out good) explains that as the dollar erodes as a store of value, people hoard alternative stores like gold and Bitcoin, suggesting these are likely successors.
arguments.conclusion_supported: Gold-backed digital money and Bitcoin are likely successors to the dollar as the dominant form of money, because evidence shows a flight from the dollar to gold and Bitcoin as stores of value.

arguments.premise_synthesis: People deposited gold with goldsmiths and received paper receipts redeemable for gold. These receipts began circulating as money. Goldsmiths issued more receipts than gold on hand (fractional reserve banking), which is contractual fraud and leads to bank runs and economic busts. Governments eventually nationalized banks, centralized gold, confiscated gold from citizens, and defaulted on redemption obligations, leaving the world with irredeemable government paper money (fiat).
arguments.conclusion_supported: The fiat monetary system is inherently unstable because it originated from contractual fraud (fractional reserve banking) and was sustained by government coercion and default, eroding trust in money.
